title: Adversaries: without the Church Scripture is doubtful and uncertain
source_text: XV. Praeterea Scripturae authoritatem quoad nos ab authoritate Ecclesiae pendere Pontificii sic probare contendunt. Absque authoritate & testimonio Ecclesiae, Scriptura nobis est dubia & incerta, & illam per Ecclesiae authoritatem & testimonium confirmari necesse est. Scripturam autem esse dubiam & incertam, nisi Ecclesiae authoritas & testimonium accedat, inde probant, quod absque authoritate illa certo sciri non potest, qui sint libri sacri & divini, qui minus. Et hoc quia plurima scripta, ab haereticis & vanis hominibus conficta, Prophetis & Apostolis afficta & supposita sunt. Nec etiam quaecunque scripserunt Prophetae & Apostoli divinam authoritatem habere meruerunt. Etenim multa leguntur scripsisse Salomo, & alii Prophetae, quae in sacrarum literarum numero habita non sunt. Tum quoque vix est ullus Scripturae sacrae liber cujus authoritas non sit in dubium vocata, aut in totum negata, ab iis qui se Christianos profitebantur. Exempli causa, Manichaei Veteris Testamenti authoritatem negabant, Ptolomaïtae librorum Mosis, Marcionitae Evangeliorum, excepto solius Lucae Evangelio, & ita de caeteris. Et adhuc hodie inter nos & Pontificios de quorundam librorum divinorum authoritate certatur. Siquidem plures libros, quos Apocryphos censemus, ad Canonem Veteris Testamenti pertinere volunt. Atque etiam de multis Novi Testamenti libris inter ipsos orthodoxos olim dubitatum est, & hodie quoque dubitatur inter eos qui ab Ecclesia Romana postremis hisce saeculis secesserunt. Ut ex. gr. de Epistola Judae & Jacobi, & quibusdam Joannis & Petri Epistolis. Adde quod libri sacri ab haereticis corrupti, depravati & interpolati sunt, iisque multa addita vel detracta. Et quibusdam adhuc suspecta est prima pars capitis octavi Evangelii secundum Joannem, ubi habetur historia de muliere adultera. In tanta ergo, inquiunt, sententiarum varietate & confusione de libris sacris & eorum partibus, qua certa ratione verum poterit inveniri absque authoritate & judicio Ecclesiae? Unde scitis libros eos qui Prophetis & Apostolis tribuuntur revera eorum esse: Et posito quod libri isti revera quosdam ex Prophetis & Apostolis habeant authores, unde certo scietis illos non fuisse scriptos humana diligentia, sed divina inspiratione, & ad nos usque integros pervenisse, non vero variis modis ab haereticis corruptos. Atque inde concludunt, ut fides nostra de Scriptura firmum fundamentum habeat, necessario recurrendum esse ad authoritatem Ecclesiae, quae scilicet, suo judicio certo & infallibili libros divinos discernit ab Apocryphis & supposititiis, & quo judicio licet fidelibus secure niti.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover the Pontificians contend to prove thus that Scripture's authority as regards us depends on the Church's authority. Without the Church's authority and testimony, Scripture is doubtful and uncertain for us, and it is necessary that it be confirmed by the Church's authority and testimony. But that Scripture is doubtful and uncertain unless the Church's authority and testimony come to it, they prove from this: that without that authority it cannot be known for certain which books are sacred and divine, and which are not. And this because very many writings, fabricated by heretics and vain men, have been fastened upon and foisted onto the Prophets and Apostles. Nor did whatever the Prophets and Apostles wrote deserve to have divine authority. For many things are read that Solomon and other Prophets wrote which were not held in the number of the sacred letters. Then also there is scarcely any book of sacred Scripture whose authority has not been called into doubt, or denied altogether, by those who professed themselves Christians. For example, the Manichaeans denied the authority of the Old Testament; the Ptolemaeans that of the books of Moses; the Marcionites that of the Gospels, except only Luke's Gospel; and so of the rest. And still today between us and the Pontificians there is contest about the authority of certain divine books. For they want several books that we judge Apocryphal to belong to the Canon of the Old Testament. And also about many books of the New Testament there was once doubt among the orthodox themselves, and today also there is doubt among those who in these last centuries have seceded from the Roman Church — for example about the Epistle of Jude and of James, and certain Epistles of John and of Peter. Add that the sacred books have been corrupted, depraved, and interpolated by heretics, and many things added to them or taken away. And to some the first part of the eighth chapter of the Gospel according to John is still suspect, where the history of the adulterous woman is had. In so great a variety and confusion of opinions, then, they say, about the sacred books and their parts, by what certain reason will the truth be able to be found without the Church's authority and judgment? Whence do you know that those books attributed to the Prophets and Apostles are truly theirs? And granted that those books truly have some of the Prophets and Apostles as authors, whence will you know for certain that they were not written by human diligence but by divine inspiration, and have come down to us intact, and not been corrupted in various ways by heretics? And from this they conclude that, so that our faith concerning Scripture may have a firm foundation, one must necessarily have recourse to the Church's authority, which by its certain and infallible judgment distinguishes divine books from Apocryphal and forged ones, and on which judgment the faithful may securely rely.
pass_b_english: The Roman doctors next try to prove that Scripture's authority for us hangs on the Church's.
Without the Church's authority and witness, they say, Scripture is doubtful and uncertain for us, and must be confirmed by that authority and witness.

They argue that without it we cannot know for certain which books are holy and divine: heretics and idle men have forged many writings under the Prophets' and Apostles' names; not everything Prophets and Apostles wrote earned divine authority (Solomon and others wrote things never numbered among the sacred letters); and scarcely any biblical book has escaped doubt or outright denial from professing Christians.

The Manichaeans rejected the Old Testament; the Ptolemaeans Moses; the Marcionites the Gospels except Luke alone — and so on. We still contest Rome over certain books they force into the Old Testament canon as Apocrypha. Even among the orthodox there was once doubt about many New Testament books, and there is still doubt among those who have left Rome in these later centuries — Jude, James, and some letters of John and Peter.
Add corruption, depravation, and interpolation by heretics, with additions and omissions; some still suspect the first part of John 8 and the story of the adulterous woman.

In so great a clash of opinions about the sacred books and their parts, they ask, how can truth be found without the Church's authority and judgment? How do you know those books are truly the Prophets' and Apostles'? And even if they are, how do you know they were written by divine inspiration rather than human care, and have reached us whole rather than variously corrupted?

They conclude that for faith about Scripture to rest on a firm base we must turn to the Church, which by a certain and infallible judgment tells divine books from Apocrypha and forgeries — a judgment the faithful may safely trust.
